rules.title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protections: just cause, relocation assistance, right of first offer and buyouts (S.D. Mun. Code ch. 9, art. 8, div. 7)
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not terminate a tenancy (a right to occupy for more than 30 days) without just cause.

At-fault causes: nonpayment; breach of a material lease term; nuisance; waste; refusal to sign a substantially similar extension; criminal activity; criminal threats; unauthorized assignment or sublet; refusal of lawful entry; unlawful use; an employee or licensee failing to vacate; failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice. For a curable violation, the landlord must first give written notice and an opportunity to cure, and may then serve a three-day notice to quit.

No-fault causes, taken in good faith:
- Owner or relative move-in for at least 12 months. For leases entered on or after June 24, 2023, this is allowed only if the lease allows it or the tenant agrees in writing. The occupant must move in within 90 days, or the unit must be re-offered to the tenant.
- Withdrawal from the rental market.
- A government, court or ordinance vacate order.
- Demolition or substantial remodel. Permits must be posted and secured, and a certified notice is required.

No-fault notice: 30 or 60 days' written notice under Civ. Code § 1946.1, in at least 12-point font. The notice must state the basis, the relocation assistance and the 5-year right to an offer to renew.

Relocation assistance, regardless of the tenant's income or length of tenancy: 2 months' actual rent, or 3 months if the tenant is a senior (62+) or disabled. It is paid directly within 15 days of the notice or given as a waiver of the final months' rent. It is in addition to the deposit refund and is credited against other legally required relocation assistance.

Right of first offer: if the unit is re-offered within 5 years after a (b)(1), (3) or (4) eviction, the displaced tenant must be offered it first. The tenant must ask in writing within 30 days of the notice and has 30 days to accept.

Notice to the Housing Commission: due within 3 business days of an at-fault or no-fault termination notice. This duty applies only 30 days after the Commission announces a submission portal.

Tenant notice: landlords must give covered tenants a written protections notice and the Commission's Tenant Protection Guide.

Buyouts: a written disclosure is required before any buyout offer. Buyout agreements must be in writing with 14-point bold statements, and must be for more than the required relocation amount, or they are void.

Other rules: retaliation is prohibited. Non-compliance voids the termination notice.

Remedies:
- Injunctive and equitable relief, and money damages including punitive damages.
- At least 3x actual economic damages for wrongful eviction.
- At least 3x the required relocation assistance plus actual damages for failure to pay it.
- Discretionary attorney's fees.
- An affirmative defense in an unlawful detainer action.
- City enforcement.
rules.key_value: No-fault relocation: 2 months' actual rent (3 months for seniors 62+ or disabled tenants), paid within 15 days or as a rent waiver; 30/60-day notice (Civ. Code § 1946.1); 5-year right of first offer (30 days to accept); wrongful eviction damages at least 3x actual economic damages; failure to pay relocation at least 3x the assistance plus actual damages

coverage.summary: Tenancies of more than 30 days in residential rental property in the City of San Diego, including mobilehome park units. Fixed-term leases of 3 months or less are not covered. Exempt: housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes), plus the listed exempt property types and owner situations.
coverage.owner_conditions: Exempt: a landlord-occupied single-family residence renting no more than two bedrooms, two ADUs or two JADUs. Exempt: a duplex where the landlord occupies one unit as principal residence from the start of the tenancy and continues to. Exempt: a separately alienable unit whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member or mobilehome park management, and that gave the prescribed written notice.
coverage.other_conditions: Also exempt: transient and tourist hotel occupancy, short-term residential occupancy, and mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law. Unlike state law, there is no 12-month occupancy threshold: any tenancy of more than 30 days is covered.

rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy; short-term residential occupancy; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing (Section 8 not exempt); mobilehomes subject to the MRL; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, RCFE, adult residential facility and non-profit transitional housing; school dormitories; shared bath or kitchen with a resident landlord; owner-occupied single-family residence (up to two bedrooms, ADUs or JADUs); owner-occupied duplex; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable property with a qualifying non-corporate landlord and written notice.

rules.quoted_span: A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause.
rules.review_note:
Precedence: the ordinance was adopted after Sept. 1, 2019, so under Civ. Code § 1946.2(i) it applies instead of state just cause only if it is more protective and contains a binding finding saying so. It is facially more protective: it covers tenancies over 30 days and gives 2–3 months' relocation versus 1 month under state law. Its purpose clause cites § 1946.2, but the ordinance findings are not in the captured code text. Verify the binding finding.

Commission portal: the Legal Aid fact sheet (Sept. 2023) estimated a July 2024 launch. Whether the portal has launched by the query date is not shown in the documents.

New construction: the 15-year certificate-of-occupancy exemption is rolling, so building eligibility changes over time.

No amendments after O-21769 N.S. (3-2024 code version) are reflected.
rules.source_notes:
Official municipal code text (D073, 3-2024 version) governs. The Legal Aid fact sheet (DX17, secondary) agrees on the main rules.

DX17 adds that neither duplex unit may be an ADU or JADU. That qualifier does not appear in § 98.0703(j) of the code. DX17 also describes the single-family exemption as 'two units or bedrooms'. The code text governs both points.

The cell candidate's figure of 3 months' relocation for all tenants came from a 2021 City summary of the earlier ordinance (D085, not provided). It is superseded by § 98.0706(c): 2 months, or 3 for seniors and disabled tenants. The cell candidate's rolling 'construction_cutoff' is expressed here as the 15-year new_construction_exemption.

rules.title: San Diego Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing (S.D. Mun. Code ch. 9, art. 8, div. 11)
rules.requirement:
Prohibitions (§ 98.1103):
- No person may sell, license or otherwise provide an algorithmic device to a landlord.
- No landlord may use an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property.

An algorithmic device is software or a product that uses algorithms to perform calculations of nonpublic competitor data to advise a landlord on, or recommend to a landlord, rental rates or occupancy levels for San Diego residential rental property. Nonpublic competitor data covers non-public information on actual rents, rent changes, supply, occupancy or lease dates, whether or not anonymized.

Each month a landlord's use continues, and each residential rental property where a device is used, is a separate violation.

Remedies (§ 98.1104):
- A tenant may sue a landlord for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
- A prevailing tenant, including one granted injunctive relief, recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Lease clauses limiting fee recovery are unenforceable.
- Remedies are cumulative.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each property is a separate violation; prevailing tenant recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees

coverage.summary: Citywide in San Diego. Applies to landlords of residential rental property and to any person who sells, licenses or provides algorithmic devices to them. No unit-count, building-age or owner-occupancy limits are stated.
coverage.other_conditions: Landlord, lease, residential rental property and tenant take their definitions from S.D. Mun. Code § 98.0702. The Division 7 exemptions in § 98.0703 are not incorporated, so there is no 15-year new-construction or owner-occupancy exemption. Applies only to software using nonpublic competitor data.

rules.exemptions: Not an 'algorithmic device': (a) software that publishes reports on rental rates or occupancy from aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old, or from public information, and does not recommend rates or occupancy for future leases or renewals; (b) software used to set rental rates or income limits under local, state or federal affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.effective_date_note: The ordinance takes effect on the 30th day after final passage. The official materials (staff report issued Feb. 27, 2025) leave the ordinance number and date of final passage blank. The Morgan Lewis alert of Aug. 21, 2026 lists the codified §§ 98.1101–98.1104 as 'effective June 2025' (month only), so no exact day can be given.

rules.review_note: Status is in_force because a later secondary source (Aug. 2026) cites the codified San Diego Mun. Code §§ 98.1101–98.1104 as effective June 2025, and reports a pending tenant suit under § 98.1103 (Keller v. UDR Inc., S.D. Cal.). A code-publisher page for codified § 98.1103 is listed as link-only (D074). The official documents captured are only the pre-adoption draft, with no final ordinance number, passage date or adoption certificate. Confirm the adopted ordinance number, the passage date and that the adopted text matches the draft. The state Cartwright Act common-pricing-algorithm rule (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729, AB 325) operates alongside; the documents do not address any interaction.
rules.source_notes: Text is taken from the official staff report and draft ordinance (D076; DX05 is the same document at the same URL). The ordinance, digest and strikeout versions are identical. Earlier candidates marked the measure 'pending' only because the draft blanks were unfilled. The Aug. 2026 Morgan Lewis alert (DX06) shows the same Division 11 was enacted and codified, so the draft and the enacted law are one measure. It is not a separate pending measure.
